R054-01.notes: B captures paragraph 1 (costs folded into rents, projects killed) + paragraph 2 (driving default) + conclusion that builders should decide. A: Passage A never calls for raising minimums. C: this is Passage B's position, not A's. D: directly contradicted ('Builders have not stopped providing parking').

R054-02.notes: Near-verbatim: 'provided less of it in places where residents can walk or take transit.' A contradicted ('have not stopped providing parking'). B: no claim they built more than required. D: not mentioned.

R054-03.notes: 'that cost is folded into rents and prices whether or not a tenant owns a car.' A: cost is folded into rent, not a separate fee. B: street-parking crowding is Passage B's concern and irrelevant to a carless tenant. C: absurd, no such requirement.

R054-04.notes: 'in dense neighborhoods with frequent trains and buses, I find it persuasive. But most Americans do not live in such places' and criticizes eliminating minimums everywhere. B: B calls their case strong and says old rules shouldn't stay. C: B opposes eliminating everywhere at once. D: no such charge made.

R054-05.notes: The line rebuts the idea that no on-site parking means no car; residents still own cars and park on the street ('the cars of its residents do not disappear'). A: no claim about preferring to live near stations. C: overstates; the point is infrequent buses, not unwillingness. D: opposite of the point being made.

R054-06.notes: Cars 'spill onto nearby blocks' = spread/overflow outward. A 'pour' is the literal-liquid trap. B 'drop' and D 'waste' do not fit cars extending onto other blocks.

R054-07.notes: Paraphrases 'lower minimums where transit is strong and to tie any remaining requirements to how often buses actually run.' B contradicted ('None of this means that the old rules should stay as they are'). C contradicted by final sentence. D: B says codes demand too many spaces, not too few.

R054-08.notes: B: 'Many codes demand far more spaces than buildings ever fill.' A: builders, once free, provided less parking near transit and rejects 'any single number written into a code,' implying codes mismatch need. A: B rejects removal everywhere. B: B says the opposite (cars don't disappear); A doesn't claim this either. C: A explicitly trusts builders.

R054-09.notes: B's core objection is spillover: residents' cars crowd nearby blocks and harm longtime residents, which is a cost outside the builder's decision. So B would answer that builder choice ignores costs imposed on neighbors. Requires inference but is the only option grounded in B. A: 'always' extreme; B says codes (not builders) demand too much. B: lots are A's point, B never addresses it. D: B ties requirements to bus frequency but never says builders can't estimate ridership.

flags.note: Passage A never explicitly says one approach fits every neighborhood; indeed A notes builders provided different amounts in transit areas. The key relies on reading A's endorsement of eliminating minimums (generally) as the 'uniform rule' B attacks. Still clearly the best of four, since A, C, D are facts B doesn't dispute, but option wording could be tightened to e.g. 'That eliminating minimums is the right policy for every city.'

R054-10.notes: B's final sentence attacks 'eliminating minimums everywhere at once' as another uniform rule, i.e., A's general prescription. A: B never disputes garage cost. C: B doesn't dispute the rules' original purpose. D: B doesn't dispute that cities eliminated minimums.

R054-11.notes: 'The next Sunday I decided to find out' (whether he was letting her win or no longer seeing the board), then 'I ... waited.' The test is whether he notices and takes the queen. A: the motive is investigation, not compensation (the later loss is incidental). B: no such intent. C: no reading of a sacrifice mentioned.
